newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italian markets drive on after rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italian markets drive on after rate cut.

text.p: Italian financial markets, already bouyant and flush with liquidity, were caught on the hop by the timing of the Bank of Italy's long-awaited interest rate cut but rose further on Wednesday expecting another reduction soon.
"The only surprise was the timing, the markets had been expecting a cut for at least a month," said Oriano Moro, equity trader with Gestnord brokers in Milan.
The central bank on Tuesday night cut key rates to a 22-year low, shaving 75 basis points off the discount rate to 6.75 percent and its Lombard rate to 8.25 percent.

The reduction, taking effect Wednesday, followed preliminary inflation data from 11 sample Italian cities which pointed to consumer prices rising 2.6 percent year-on-year in January, unchanged on the previous two months but better than expected.
The central bank's rate cut was not perceived by investors to be its last in the cycle. Analysts generally expected to see another 75 basis point cut in the second quarter.
Shares powered ahead, driven by a fresh wave of liquidity. At 1150 GMT the Mib30 blue chip index was up 1.69 percent and all-share Mibtel index up 1.73 percent, but off opening highs.
"This is a liquidity-driven market that wants good news and it got good news," said David Fisher, a broker at CIMO in Milan.

Italian bonds and futures tempered their opening enthusiasm after tearing higher to a fresh record high on the March LIFFE future. The March future contract was quoted 44 basis points higher at 132.17 after hitting an early peak of 132.30.

Markets had been expecting monetary policy to ease but not until metalworkers and employers reached an accord on wage contracts in a long-running dispute. Analysts said hopes of an early accord were boosted by news Prime Minister Romano Prodi planned to meet unions and management.

"Btps are up but not as wildly as some might have expected," said Luca Jellinek at Paribas in London. Italian bond markets have been euphoric recently on expectations Prodi will have little trouble in pushing through a supplementary mini-budget in spring to get state accounts ready for Italy's date with Europe.
The lira had strengthened past 970 per mark early but settled back to 970.80 as the morning wore on.
The Milan stock exchange has seen massive liquidity inflows so far this year as domestic investors have begun to switch out of lower-yielding government debt into shares.

"There's nothing negative at the moment, it's all good news. The mini-budget and metalworkers' accord have been taken for granted. If you're short you're going to get caught, so go with the flow, that's the byword," said Moro.
Several securities houses have forecast the Italian stock market could see a further 20 percent uptick by March.
Moro noted that there were few signs yet of major foreign order inflows. "The interest is there but they haven't jumped in with both feet yet, it's just a nibble so far."
Equity analysts said U.S. portfolios had been low in Italian stocks. "But if Wall Street hits a bit of crisis they could move in," Moro said. He saw a fresh rate cut as early as February.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio said he had cut rates because the time was right but warned he still had a "stick" at the ready if conditions changed.

"I dropped my guard because current conditions allowed it but I'm waiting to see what happens in the next few weeks and I always have a stick firmly in my hand," La Stampa quoted him as saying on Wednesday.
